notes:
1. Basic Facts

This chapter covers three major physiographic divisions of India:

  • The Indian Desert.
  • The Coastal Plains.
  • The Islands.

These regions differ greatly in relief, climate, drainage, soils, vegetation, settlement and economic importance.

2. Indian Desert — Basic Facts
  • The Indian Desert is commonly called the Thar Desert.
  • It lies mainly in western Rajasthan.
  • It extends into adjoining Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab to a smaller extent.
  • The desert continues westward into Pakistan.
  • It lies mainly to the west of the Aravalli Range.
  • It is part of the larger arid region of northwestern South Asia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Indian Desert → Thar Desert → Mainly Rajasthan

3. Location of the Thar Desert

The Thar Desert is bounded broadly by:

  • Aravalli Range to the east.
  • Punjab Plain toward the north.
  • Rann of Kachchh toward the south.
  • Pakistan's desert region toward the west.
4. Aravalli and the Desert
  • Aravalli runs roughly southwest to northeast.
  • Much of the range lies parallel rather than perpendicular to the southwest monsoon winds.
  • It therefore provides limited orographic uplift to moisture-bearing Arabian Sea winds.
  • This is one factor contributing to the aridity of western Rajasthan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aravalli Orientation → Weak Barrier to Southwest Monsoon

5. Rainfall in the Indian Desert
  • Rainfall is very low and highly variable.
  • Much of western Rajasthan receives less than about 250 mm annually.
  • Rainfall decreases generally toward the west.
  • Droughts are frequent.
  • Most rainfall occurs during the southwest monsoon season.
6. Temperature Characteristics
  • Summers are extremely hot.
  • Day temperatures may become very high.
  • Nights can be much cooler because dry air and clear skies permit rapid heat loss.
  • Winters can become quite cold, especially at night.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Desert Climate → High Diurnal Temperature Range

7. Aridity

Aridity results from:

  • Low rainfall.
  • High evaporation.
  • Continental location.
  • Sparse vegetation.
  • Limited moisture supply.
  • Unfavourable orientation of the Aravalli to monsoon winds.
8. Desert Surface

The Thar contains:

  • Sandy plains.
  • Sand dunes.
  • Rocky surfaces.
  • Gravel plains.
  • Saline depressions.
  • Seasonal river channels.
9. Sand Dunes
  • Sand dunes are hills or ridges formed by wind-deposited sand.
  • Wind transports and deposits sand where velocity decreases.
  • Dune forms vary with wind direction and vegetation.
10. Barchans
  • Barchans are crescent-shaped sand dunes.
  • Their horns point downwind.
  • They commonly develop where sand supply is limited and winds blow mainly from one direction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Barchan → Crescent-Shaped Dune

11. Longitudinal Dunes
  • Longitudinal dunes form long ridges roughly parallel to the prevailing wind direction.
  • They are common in parts of the Thar Desert.
12. Transverse Dunes
  • Transverse dunes form ridges roughly perpendicular to the prevailing wind direction.
  • They develop where sand supply is abundant.
13. Wind Erosion

Major wind-erosion processes include:

  • Deflation.
  • Abrasion.
  • Attrition.
14. Deflation
  • Deflation is removal of loose fine particles by wind.
  • It can leave behind coarser gravel surfaces.
15. Abrasion
  • Wind-driven sand erodes exposed rock surfaces.
  • This mechanical wearing is called abrasion.
16. Desert Pavement
  • Removal of fine particles can leave a surface covered by stones and gravel.
  • Such surfaces are sometimes called desert pavement.
17. Luni River
  • Luni is the most important river of the Indian Desert region.
  • It rises near the Aravalli region around Ajmer.
  • It flows southwestward across Rajasthan.
  • It ends in the marshy Rann of Kachchh rather than reaching the open sea through a major permanent channel.
  • Its lower course becomes increasingly saline.
📌 Must-Memorise

Important Thar River → Luni

18. Inland Drainage
  • Much of western Rajasthan has inland drainage.
  • Streams may terminate in lakes, marshes or sandy depressions.
  • Many channels are seasonal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thar Desert → Inland Drainage Common

19. Seasonal Streams
  • Many desert streams flow only after rainfall.
  • They remain dry for much of the year.
  • Such temporary streams are characteristic of arid climates.
20. Salt Lakes

Important saline lakes of Rajasthan include:

  • Sambhar.
  • Didwana.
  • Pachpadra.
  • Lunkaransar.
21. Sambhar Lake
  • Sambhar Lake lies in Rajasthan.
  • It is India's largest inland salt lake in standard geography references.
  • It is an important centre of salt production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Largest Inland Salt Lake of India → Sambhar

22. Desert Soils
  • Desert soils are generally sandy and low in organic matter.
  • Some contain soluble salts.
  • Irrigation can make parts of the desert agriculturally productive.
  • Poor drainage under irrigation can also cause salinity.
23. Desert Vegetation

Typical vegetation includes:

  • Thorny shrubs.
  • Acacia.
  • Prosopis.
  • Cacti-like succulents.
  • Grasses adapted to dry conditions.
  • Plants show xerophytic adaptations.
24. Xerophytic Adaptations

Common adaptations include:

  • Reduced leaves or spines.
  • Deep root systems.
  • Thick waxy cuticle.
  • Water-storage tissues.
  • Reduced transpiration.
25. Desert Animals

Important animals include:

  • Camel.
  • Chinkara.
  • Desert fox.
  • Great Indian Bustard.
  • Blackbuck in suitable dry grasslands.
  • Various reptiles.
26. Great Indian Bustard
  • Great Indian Bustard is a large ground-dwelling bird of arid and semi-arid grasslands.
  • Rajasthan contains important remaining habitat.
  • It is one of India's most threatened birds.
27. Camel
  • Camel is highly adapted to arid conditions.
  • It can tolerate substantial dehydration.
  • Broad padded feet help movement on sand.
  • It is traditionally important for transport in desert regions.
28. Indira Gandhi Canal
  • The Indira Gandhi Canal has transformed parts of western Rajasthan.
  • It brings water from the Sutlej-Beas river system into arid areas.
  • It supports irrigation, drinking-water supply and settlement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Indira Gandhi Canal → Rajasthan Desert Irrigation

29. Effects of Irrigation in Desert

Benefits include:

  • Expansion of agriculture.
  • Settlement growth.
  • Drinking-water availability.
  • Increased cropping.

Possible problems include:

  • Waterlogging.
  • Soil salinity.
  • Ecological change.
30. Desert Agriculture

With irrigation, crops include:

  • Wheat.
  • Mustard.
  • Cotton.
  • Bajra.
  • Pulses.

In drier rain-fed areas:

  • Bajra is particularly important.
31. Bajra
  • Bajra or pearl millet is drought-resistant.
  • It is well suited to arid and semi-arid climates.
  • Rajasthan is an important producing region.
32. Rann of Kachchh
  • The Rann of Kachchh lies mainly in Gujarat.
  • It is a vast seasonal salt marsh.
  • It becomes inundated during parts of the monsoon.
  • During the dry season, large salt-encrusted surfaces develop.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rann of Kachchh → Seasonal Salt Marsh

33. Great Rann and Little Rann

The Rann region is commonly divided into:

  • Great Rann of Kachchh.
  • Little Rann of Kachchh.
34. Little Rann of Kachchh
  • The Little Rann is famous for the Indian Wild Ass.
  • The Wild Ass Sanctuary is located here.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Wild Ass → Little Rann of Kachchh

35. Desertification
  • Desertification means land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions.
  • Causes include:
  • Overgrazing.
  • Deforestation.
  • Wind erosion.
  • Unsustainable cultivation.
  • Poor irrigation practices.
  • Climate variability.
36. Coastal Plains — Basic Classification

India has two major coastal plains:

  • Western Coastal Plain.
  • Eastern Coastal Plain.

They differ in width, drainage, landforms and river mouths.

37. Western Coastal Plain
  • The Western Coastal Plain lies between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.
  • It is generally narrow.
  • The Western Ghats rise close to the coast.
  • Many west-flowing rivers are short and swift.
  • Estuaries are common.
📌 Must-Memorise

Western Coast → Narrow + Estuaries

38. Width of Western Coastal Plain
  • Width varies considerably.
  • It is generally narrower than the eastern coastal plain.
  • Some sections are only a few tens of kilometres wide.
39. Major Divisions of Western Coastal Plain

From north to south:

  • Gujarat Coast.
  • Konkan Coast.
  • Kanara/Karnataka Coast.
  • Malabar Coast.

Some textbook classifications focus mainly on Konkan, Kanara and Malabar south of Gujarat.

40. Gujarat Coast

Important features include:

  • Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Kathiawar/Saurashtra Peninsula.
  • Extensive tidal flats.
  • Salt marshes.
41. Gulf of Kachchh
  • Gulf of Kachchh lies in northwestern Gujarat.
  • It opens into the Arabian Sea.
  • It has strong tidal influence.
  • Coral reefs and marine habitats occur in parts of the gulf.
42. Gulf of Khambhat
  • Gulf of Khambhat lies south of the Saurashtra Peninsula.
  • Rivers such as Narmada and Tapi enter this region.
  • It experiences strong tides.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narmada + Tapi → Gulf of Khambhat Region

43. Saurashtra Peninsula
  • Saurashtra or Kathiawar Peninsula lies in Gujarat.
  • It projects into the Arabian Sea.
  • Girnar Hills occur in this region.
44. Konkan Coast
  • Konkan Coast extends mainly along Maharashtra and Goa.
  • It lies between the Western Ghats and Arabian Sea.
  • The coast is relatively narrow and dissected.
  • Creeks and estuaries are common.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Konkan → Maharashtra + Goa

45. Mumbai and Konkan
  • Mumbai lies on the Konkan coast.
  • Its natural harbour helped the development of a major port.
  • Numerous creeks and inlets characterise the surrounding coast.
46. Kanara Coast
  • Kanara or Karnataka Coast lies mainly along Karnataka.
  • It is narrow.
  • Several short west-flowing rivers descend rapidly from the Western Ghats.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kanara → Karnataka

47. Malabar Coast
  • Malabar Coast lies mainly along Kerala.
  • It is broader in some sectors than the Konkan and Kanara coasts.
  • Lagoons and backwaters are major features.
  • Coconut cultivation is widespread.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malabar → Kerala → Backwaters

48. Kerala Backwaters
  • Kerala's backwaters consist of lagoons, lakes and interconnected canals.
  • They are locally called kayals.
  • Many lie parallel to the coast.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kerala Backwaters → Kayals

49. Vembanad Lake
  • Vembanad is the largest lake in Kerala.
  • It is a major backwater lagoon system.
  • It extends across several districts.
  • It is connected with the Arabian Sea through channels.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vembanad → Kerala Backwater

50. Ashtamudi Lake
  • Ashtamudi is an important backwater lake in Kerala.
  • It lies near Kollam.
  • It has a distinctive branching shape.
51. Western Coast Estuaries
  • Many short west-flowing rivers form estuaries.
  • Major rivers Narmada and Tapi also reach the Arabian Sea through estuarine mouths.
  • Strong tidal influence prevents extensive delta formation in many areas.
52. Why Large Deltas Are Rare on Western Coast

Reasons include:

  • Narrow coastal plain.
  • Steep gradient.
  • Short river courses.
  • Strong tidal action.
  • Relatively lower sediment deposition near mouths.
53. Eastern Coastal Plain
  • Eastern Coastal Plain lies between the Eastern Ghats and Bay of Bengal.
  • It is generally broader than the Western Coastal Plain.
  • Major rivers form extensive deltas.
  • The coast is more depositional.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eastern Coast → Broad + Deltas

54. Major Divisions of Eastern Coastal Plain

Traditional divisions include:

  • Northern Circars.
  • Coromandel Coast.
55. Northern Circars
  • Northern Circars are associated mainly with the coastal plains of Andhra Pradesh and adjoining Odisha sectors.
  • Large river deltas dominate much of this coast.
56. Coromandel Coast
  • Coromandel Coast lies along southeastern India.
  • It is strongly associated with Tamil Nadu.
  • It faces the Bay of Bengal.
  • It receives substantial rainfall from the northeast monsoon.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu East Coast → Coromandel Coast

57. Major East-Flowing Rivers

Important rivers reaching the eastern coast include:

  • Mahanadi.
  • Godavari.
  • Krishna.
  • Kaveri.

These rivers have built extensive alluvial deltas.

58. Mahanadi Delta
  • Mahanadi forms a large delta in Odisha.
  • The deltaic plain is fertile.
  • The lower coast is vulnerable to cyclones and floods.
59. Godavari Delta
  • Godavari forms a major delta in Andhra Pradesh.
  • It has several distributaries.
  • The region is agriculturally productive.
60. Krishna Delta
  • Krishna forms another major delta in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Together, the Krishna and Godavari deltas form an extensive fertile coastal region.
61. Kaveri Delta
  • Kaveri forms a major delta in Tamil Nadu.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's most important agricultural regions.
  • Rice cultivation is particularly important.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kaveri Delta → Tamil Nadu → Rice

62. Delta Formation

A delta forms when:

  • River carries sediment.
  • River velocity falls near the sea.
  • Sediment is deposited.
  • River splits into distributaries.
63. Why Eastern Coast Has Large Deltas

Reasons include:

  • Broad coastal plain.
  • Gentle gradients.
  • Long east-flowing rivers.
  • Large sediment loads.
  • Favourable depositional conditions.
64. Important Lagoons on Eastern Coast

Important examples include:

  • Chilika Lake.
  • Pulicat Lake.
  • Kolleru Lake, though Kolleru is primarily a freshwater lake between deltaic systems rather than a coastal lagoon in the strict sense.
65. Chilika Lake
  • Chilika lies in Odisha.
  • It is a large brackish-water lagoon.
  • It is connected with the Bay of Bengal.
  • It is famous for migratory birds and fisheries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chilika → Odisha → Brackish Lagoon

66. Pulicat Lake
  • Pulicat Lake lies along the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu coast.
  • It is a brackish-water lagoon.
  • Sriharikota separates much of it from the Bay of Bengal.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Pulicat → Andhra Pradesh + Tamil Nadu

67. Sriharikota
  • Sriharikota is a barrier island between Pulicat Lake and the Bay of Bengal.
  • India's major space-launch centre is located there.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sriharikota → Pulicat Lake Barrier Island

68. Kolleru Lake
  • Kolleru Lake lies in Andhra Pradesh.
  • It lies between the Krishna and Godavari delta regions.
  • It is primarily a freshwater lake.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Kolleru → Freshwater

Chilika/Pulicat → Brackish

69. Coastline and Cyclones
  • The eastern coast is more exposed to tropical cyclones from the Bay of Bengal.
  • Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal are particularly vulnerable.
  • Storm surges can inundate low-lying coastal areas.
70. Storm Surge
  • A storm surge is an abnormal rise of sea level caused mainly by strong cyclone winds and low atmospheric pressure.
  • It can cause severe coastal flooding.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cyclone Coastal Hazard → Storm Surge

71. Coastal Erosion

Coastal erosion can result from:

  • Waves.
  • Storms.
  • Sea-level change.
  • Sediment deficits.
  • Human structures.
  • Removal of coastal vegetation.
72. Beaches
  • Beaches form where waves deposit sand or gravel.
  • India has extensive beaches on both coasts.
  • Beach width changes seasonally according to wave conditions.
73. Spits
  • A spit is a narrow ridge of sand extending from the coast into water.
  • It forms due to longshore sediment transport.
74. Barrier Islands
  • Barrier islands are elongated sedimentary islands lying parallel to the coast.
  • They can enclose lagoons.
  • Sriharikota is a major Indian example.
75. Lagoons
  • Lagoons are shallow water bodies partly or completely separated from the sea by sand bars, spits or barrier islands.
  • Their water may be fresh, brackish or saline depending on connections and inflow.
76. Estuary
  • An estuary is a tidal river mouth where freshwater mixes with seawater.
  • Estuaries are common along the western coast.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Estuary → Freshwater + Seawater Mixing

77. Coastal Plains and Ports

India's coastal plains contain numerous important ports because of:

  • Maritime trade.
  • Natural harbours.
  • Industrial development.
  • Connections with inland transport networks.
78. Major Western Ports — Map Awareness

Important western ports include:

  • Kandla/Deendayal.
  • Mumbai.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru Port.
  • Mormugao.
  • New Mangalore.
  • Kochi.

Detailed transport facts will be covered later.

79. Major Eastern Ports — Map Awareness

Important eastern ports include:

  • Kolkata-Haldia.
  • Paradip.
  • Visakhapatnam.
  • Chennai.
  • Kamarajar/Ennore.
  • V.O. Chidambaranar Port at Thoothukudi.
80. Tamil Nadu Coastal Divisions

Important Tamil Nadu coastal sectors include:

  • Coromandel Coast.
  • Palk Bay coast.
  • Gulf of Mannar coast.
  • Kanyakumari coastal sector.
81. Palk Bay
  • Palk Bay lies between Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.
  • It is shallow.
  • It is connected with the Palk Strait region.
  • Fishing is economically important.
82. Gulf of Mannar
  • Gulf of Mannar lies between southeastern Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.
  • It supports:
  • Coral reefs.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Mangroves.
  • Rich marine biodiversity.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Gulf of Mannar → Coral + Seagrass + Dugong Habitat

83. Rameswaram
  • Rameswaram lies on Pamban Island.
  • It is located between mainland Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.
  • It lies close to the chain of shoals known as Adam's Bridge/Rama Setu.
84. Pamban Island
  • Pamban Island lies off the Ramanathapuram coast.
  • Rameswaram is located on it.
  • Pamban channel separates it from mainland Tamil Nadu.
85. Adam's Bridge / Rama Setu
  • It is a chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka.
  • It extends from the Rameswaram region toward Mannar Island.
  • The waters are shallow.
86. Islands of India — Major Groups

India's major island groups are:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Lakshadweep Islands.

Other coastal islands also occur along both mainland coasts.

87. Andaman and Nicobar Islands
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie east/southeast of mainland India.
  • They form a long north-south chain.
  • They lie between the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea.
  • They are mainly tectonic island-arc features.
  • Some islands have volcanic origin.
88. Number and Distribution — Concept
  • The archipelago contains hundreds of islands, islets and rocky outcrops.
  • Only a portion are inhabited.
  • The Andaman group lies north of the Nicobar group.
89. Ten Degree Channel
  • Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman group from the Nicobar group.
  • It lies close to 10° N latitude.
📌 Must-Memorise

10° Channel → Andaman / Nicobar

90. Andaman Group

Important islands include:

  • North Andaman.
  • Middle Andaman.
  • South Andaman.
  • Little Andaman.
91. Great Andaman
  • North, Middle and South Andaman together form the main Great Andaman landmass separated by narrow channels.
92. Duncan Passage
  • Duncan Passage separates South Andaman from Little Andaman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Duncan Passage → South Andaman / Little Andaman

93. Nicobar Group

Important islands include:

  • Car Nicobar.
  • Nancowry group.
  • Little Nicobar.
  • Great Nicobar.
94. Great Nicobar
  • Great Nicobar is the largest island in the Nicobar group.
  • Indira Point lies at its southern end.
  • Great Nicobar is close to Indonesia's Sumatra region.
95. Indira Point
  • Indira Point is India's southernmost point.
  • It lies on Great Nicobar Island.
  • It was affected by land subsidence during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
📌 Must-Memorise

Southernmost India → Indira Point → Great Nicobar

96. Saddle Peak
  • Saddle Peak is the highest point in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • It lies on North Andaman Island.
  • Its elevation is about 732 metres.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

A&N Highest Point → Saddle Peak

97. Barren Island
  • Barren Island lies in the Andaman Sea.
  • It contains India's only confirmed active volcano.
  • It is part of the volcanic island arc associated with tectonic plate boundaries.
📌 Must-Memorise

India's Active Volcano → Barren Island

98. Narcondam Island
  • Narcondam is a volcanic island in the Andaman Sea.
  • It is generally regarded as dormant/extinct in standard geography treatments.
  • It is known for the endemic Narcondam Hornbill.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narcondam → Hornbill

99. Andaman-Nicobar Tectonic Setting
  • The islands are associated with an active convergent plate boundary.
  • Their geological setting continues southward toward Indonesia.
  • Earthquakes and tsunamis are therefore significant hazards.
100. 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami
  • The 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake generated a massive tsunami.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands were severely affected.
  • Coastal areas of Tamil Nadu were also heavily impacted.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

2004 Tsunami → A&N + Tamil Nadu Coast Severely Affected

101. Coral Reefs in Andaman and Nicobar
  • Fringing reefs and other coral formations occur around many islands.
  • Warm tropical waters support marine biodiversity.
  • Mangroves are also extensive.
102. Mangroves in Andaman and Nicobar
  • Mangroves occur along sheltered coasts and tidal creeks.
  • They reduce coastal erosion.
  • They support fish, crustaceans and birds.
  • They provide some protection from waves and storm surges.
103. Strategic Importance of A&N

The islands are strategically important because they:

  • Lie close to major sea routes.
  • Are near Southeast Asia.
  • Overlook approaches to the Malacca Strait region.
  • Extend India's maritime presence far eastward into the Indian Ocean.
104. Malacca Strait Link
  • Malacca Strait lies between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra.
  • It is one of the world's major maritime trade routes.
  • The Andaman-Nicobar chain lies northwest of its approaches.
105. Lakshadweep Islands
  • Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea.
  • It is west of Kerala.
  • The islands are mainly coral in origin.
  • They include atolls, reefs and low coral islands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lakshadweep → Coral Islands → Arabian Sea

106. Atoll
  • An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef or island enclosing or partly enclosing a lagoon.
  • Lakshadweep contains classic atoll formations.
107. Coral Formation
  • Reef-building corals secrete calcium carbonate.
  • Coral reefs develop mainly in warm, shallow, clear marine waters.
  • Coral growth is sensitive to temperature, sediment and pollution.
108. Largest Island of Lakshadweep
  • Andrott is the largest island of Lakshadweep by area.
  • Minicoy is one of the largest and southernmost major islands.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Lakshadweep Island → Andrott

109. Minicoy Island
  • Minicoy lies in the southern part of Lakshadweep.
  • It is separated from the main Lakshadweep group by the Nine Degree Channel.
  • It is culturally and geographically distinct within the archipelago.
110. Nine Degree Channel
  • Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the main Lakshadweep group.
📌 Must-Memorise

9° Channel → Minicoy / Main Lakshadweep

111. Eight Degree Channel
  • Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives region.
📌 Must-Memorise

8° Channel → Minicoy / Maldives

112. Kavaratti
  • Kavaratti is the administrative capital of Lakshadweep.
  • It is a coral island.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lakshadweep Capital → Kavaratti

113. Agatti
  • Agatti is an important island of Lakshadweep.
  • It has an airport.
  • Coral reefs and lagoons surround the island.
114. Bangaram
  • Bangaram is a small coral island in Lakshadweep.
  • It is known for lagoon and reef tourism.
115. Lakshadweep Relief
  • The islands are very low-lying.
  • Their elevations are only a few metres above sea level.
  • This makes them vulnerable to:
  • Sea-level rise.
  • Storm surges.
  • Coastal erosion.
  • Coral-reef degradation.
116. Coral Islands vs Continental Islands

Lakshadweep:

  • Coral origin.
  • Low and flat.
  • Atolls common.

Andaman-Nicobar:

  • Tectonic island arc.
  • Rugged and elevated.
  • Volcanic features occur.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lakshadweep and Andaman-Nicobar do NOT have the same geological origin.

117. Mainland Coastal Islands

Important examples include:

  • Mumbai's original island complex.
  • Elephanta.
  • Salsette.
  • Pamban.
  • Sriharikota.
  • Abdul Kalam Island off Odisha.
  • Numerous deltaic and estuarine islands.
118. Salsette Island
  • Much of Mumbai's northern metropolitan area lies on Salsette Island.
  • Urban reclamation has greatly altered the original island geography.
119. Elephanta Island
  • Elephanta Island lies in Mumbai Harbour.
  • It is famous for rock-cut cave temples.
120. Abdul Kalam Island
  • Abdul Kalam Island lies off the Odisha coast.
  • It was formerly known as Wheeler Island.
  • It is associated with missile testing.
121. Coastal Plains and Agriculture

Western coast:

  • Coconut.
  • Rice.
  • Spices.
  • Rubber in wetter south.
  • Plantation crops.

Eastern coast:

  • Rice.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Groundnut in suitable regions.
  • Delta agriculture.
122. Coastal Fisheries
  • Coastal waters support marine fisheries.
  • Estuaries, lagoons and mangroves serve as nursery grounds.
  • Fishing is particularly important in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and other coastal states.
123. Aquaculture
  • Coastal aquaculture includes:
  • Shrimp farming.
  • Fish culture.
  • Brackish-water aquaculture.
  • Deltaic and lagoon environments are often utilised.
124. Coastal Ecosystems

Major coastal ecosystems include:

  • Mangroves.
  • Coral reefs.
  • Estuaries.
  • Lagoons.
  • Seagrass beds.
  • Mudflats.
  • Sandy beaches.
125. Mangroves
  • Mangroves are salt-tolerant coastal plants.
  • They grow mainly in intertidal muddy environments.
  • Important Indian mangrove regions include:
  • Sundarbans.
  • Mahanadi delta.

126. Pichavaram Mangroves
  • Pichavaram lies in Tamil Nadu near the Cuddalore–Chidambaram region.
  • It contains an extensive mangrove ecosystem.
  • It is associated with the Vellar-Coleroon estuarine region.

Pichavaram → Mangroves

127. Muthupet Mangroves
  • Muthupet mangroves lie along the southeastern Tamil Nadu coast.
  • They are associated with the Kaveri delta coastal region and lagoonal environment.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Muthupet → Tamil Nadu Mangroves

128. Seagrass Beds
  • Seagrasses are flowering marine plants.
  • They form underwater meadows in shallow coastal waters.
  • Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay contain important seagrass habitats.
  • Dugongs depend heavily on seagrass.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dugong → Seagrass

129. Coral Reefs of India

Major coral-reef regions include:

  • Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Gulf of Mannar.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Four Major Coral Reef Regions → Kachchh, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Mannar, A&N

130. Types of Coral Reefs

Major types include:

  • Fringing reef.
  • Barrier reef.
  • Atoll.
131. Fringing Reef
  • Fringing reefs develop close to shore.
  • They may be separated from land by a narrow lagoon.
132. Barrier Reef
  • Barrier reefs lie farther offshore.
  • A broad lagoon separates them from land.
133. Atoll Reef
  • Atolls form ring-shaped reefs around a central lagoon.
  • Lakshadweep is famous for atoll-type formations.
134. Coastal Hazards

Major hazards include:

  • Tropical cyclones.
  • Storm surges.
  • Tsunamis.
  • Coastal erosion.
  • Sea-level rise.
  • Saltwater intrusion.
135. Saltwater Intrusion
  • Saltwater intrusion occurs when seawater moves into freshwater aquifers.
  • Excessive groundwater extraction in coastal areas can worsen the problem.
136. Coastal Sand Dunes
  • Coastal dunes form when wind deposits beach sand inland.
  • Vegetation helps stabilise dunes.
  • Dunes can reduce inland movement of wind-blown sand and provide storm protection.
137. Coastal Regulation Importance
  • Coastal regions are environmentally sensitive.
  • Unplanned construction can worsen erosion, habitat loss and disaster exposure.
  • Mangroves, dunes and wetlands act as natural protective systems.
138. Western vs Eastern Coastal Plain

Western Coastal Plain:

  • Narrow.
  • Western Ghats close to coast.
  • Short swift rivers.
  • Estuaries common.
  • Backwaters especially in Kerala.

Eastern Coastal Plain:

  • Broad.
  • Major long rivers.
  • Large deltas.
  • Lagoons common.
  • Greater cyclone exposure.
139. Indian Desert vs Coastal Plains

Indian Desert:

  • Dry.
  • Inland drainage.
  • Sand dunes.
  • Sparse vegetation.

Coastal Plains:

  • Maritime influence.
  • River mouths.
  • High settlement and port concentration.
  • Marine and estuarine ecosystems.
